summary:
For farmers, choosing what to plant means balancing limited water, rising pressures on their livelihoods and the long-term health of their land. Field Rewind is an app that helps farmers understand changing growing conditions and explore crop rotations that fit their water supply and priorities.

Our interactive decision-support tool combines NASA climate records and Earth observations with local soil information and sourced crop characteristics. Farmers can compare rotations across 40 historical seasons, identify when their water supply would have fallen short of modelled crop needs, and explore scenarios with different rainfall and temperatures. Water budgets and yield assumptions help them examine irrigation affordability and estimated nutrient removal.

Maps and season-by-season visualizations make the comparisons easier to understand, while clearly labelled sources and information gaps help farmers judge what the results can support.

By making environmental data easier to understand and use, Field Rewind helps farmers make planting decisions suited to their local climate and water supply, supporting their livelihoods and protecting the land they depend on.
details:
Field Rewind turns historical environmental data into an interactive comparison of crop-rotation choices. Rather than asking farmers to interpret disconnected satellite maps, it connects their location, crop choices, available water and priorities in one workflow.

Users select a location, build two or three rotations, and choose a seasonal water supply. The app replays 40 seasons, from 1986 to 2025, using NASA POWER daily weather records. It calculates reference evapotranspiration using the FAO-56 Penman–Monteith method, applies sourced crop coefficients and growth stages, and estimates irrigation needs after effective rainfall. Interactive strips and water gauges reveal which seasons exceed the selected supply. POWER is labelled “regional climate, about 50 km grid,” making its scale clear.

A what-if panel applies rainfall and temperature adjustments to the historical record, allowing users to explore sensitivity without presenting those scenarios as forecasts. Additional tools translate a water budget into supply and compare rotations against farmer-selected priorities, including fewer water-short seasons, lower irrigation needs, crop diversity and lower nitrogen removal in harvested crops.

Field conditions provide complementary evidence through Landsat vegetation observations, NASADEM terrain, USDA soil information and available ground comparisons. We also implemented fetch-and-save access to NASA SMAP soil moisture and GPM IMERG rainfall for three demonstration locations. These dated snapshots retain their observation periods and quality information. SMAP retrievals that fail quality criteria are excluded rather than presented as reliable measurements.

Nutrient comparisons use published removal factors and user-entered yield assumptions. They help explain potential trade-offs while keeping removal distinct from nutrients remaining in the soil or demonstrated soil-health improvement. An optional Gemini summary draws on computed results, with numerical claims checked against cited data paths.

We built the application with Next.js, TypeScript, React, Leaflet and the Google GenAI SDK. The local implementation passed 921 automated tests, lint, type checking and a production build.

Our design emphasizes understandable comparisons, visible uncertainty and traceable evidence. Current crop parameters are California-based, and some soil datasets cover only the United States. Field Rewind is a prototype for exploring choices and preparing questions for local experts; it does not predict crop survival, yield or soil recovery.
